text: How to Audit Your Brand’s AI Search Visibility (Free Checklist) by Jayson DeMers | 0 comments Key Takeaways An AI visibility audit scores how often ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, and Google AI Overviews mention your brand. You can run the full seven-step audit in 6 to 10 hours with no paid tools. Off-site presence decides most outcomes: Earned and owned media supply most AI citations, though no one publishes the circulating “90%” figure. Benchmark against a 20% mention rate on category-defining prompts, and re-audit every quarter. What Is an AI Visibility Audit? An AI visibility audit is a structured check of how often, how accurately and how favorably AI answer engines mention your brand. It covers ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, and Google AI Overviews, and it records which sources each answer cites. An SEO audit checks whether your pages rank, while an AI visibility audit checks whether the answer names you. This guide gives you my seven-step framework and a free 16-point checklist. The same check goes by other names: an LLM visibility audit, an AI search audit or a GEO audit. Each one asks whether ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude and Google’s AI Overviews mention your brand, recommend it, or cite your pages with a link. Visibility state What the answer does How to log it in the audit sheet Absent Names competitors and never names you 0, plus the competitors named Mentioned Names your brand in passing or in a list 1, plus your position in the list Recommended Names you as a fit for the buyer’s stated need 2, plus the reason the answer gives Cited Links one of your pages as a source 3, plus the URL it links The core question is blunt: when your buyers ask AI for recommendations, does your brand come up? This audit answers that in 6 to 10 hours of work. Wait, don’t I need an expensive monitoring tool for this? Nope. A spreadsheet and the free chat interfaces cover the entire baseline. One frame before we start: I think of ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, and AI Overviews as the AI jury. They deliberate over sources you don’t control, then hand down verdicts your buyers treat as fact. The audit is discovery, and you’re about to find out what evidence the jury has on you. We list what an AI search audit checks, from crawler access to share of model . We run this exact audit at OutreachBloom, my B2B agency for cold email, LinkedIn outreach, and AI search visibility. What follows is the whole process, nothing held back. We also summarise what Google says you don’t need to do for AI search , quoting its own documentation. Why AI Visibility Audits Matter in 2026 Buyers moved. ChatGPT has reached 800 million weekly active users, per OpenAI (October 2025) . Google AI Overviews now appear in 25.11% of searches , a sharp rise from early 2025. Around 93% of Google AI Mode sessions end without a click, per Semrush’s study of about 69 million US desktop sessions in mid-2025. AI Mode was roughly 1% of searches in that window, and the same study put AI Overviews at 43%. Ouch. If the answer never names you, the buyer never meets you. Your Google rankings won’t save you either. Ahrefs’ August 2025 research found roughly 80% of URLs cited in AI responses don’t rank in Google’s top 100. The jury also weighs different signals than Google does. ConvertMate analyzed more than 80 million citations and found brand search volume correlates with AI citations at 0.334. Traditional domain authority showed little predictive correlation. Signals explain what the engines weigh, and our guide on why competitors get cited by ChatGPT when you are not explains what to do about it. Two terms matter before you score anything. A mention is your brand named inside an AI response. A citation is a clickable source link, typically in Perplexity, AI Overviews, or ChatGPT Search. The distinction changes your strategy, so I wrote a full guide on brand mentions vs citations if you want the deep version. Key Data Point: Earned Media Drives AI Citations Neither firm usually credited for the “90%” figure publishes it. Muck Rack has published 89% and later 84% for non-paid sources, and Fullintel has published 47% to 48%, checked September 10, 2026. The 7-Step AI Visibility Audit Framework Run these seven steps in order. Each one builds on the last, and skipping the early steps produces findings you can’t act on. Step 1: Build Your Prompt Library A prompt library is a curated set of 20 to 50 queries written the way your target buyers talk. It’s the foundation of the whole audit, so build it first. Group your prompts into four categories: Category definition: “what is X” Comparison: “X vs Y” Recommendation: “best X for Y” Use-case: “how do I solve X” Use your buyer’s phrasing instead of your internal language. “Best cold email agency for SaaS startups” beats “B2B outbound services provider” every time. Step 2: Test Across Major AI Platforms Run every prompt through ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, and Google AI Overviews. Poll the whole jury, because one juror tells you almost nothing. Citation volumes vary enormously across platforms for the same brand, per Superlines’ analysis of 34,234 AI responses. So document the full response from each platform. A yes or no on appearance throws away the data you’ll need later. Before you shortlist a tracker, check who writes the AI visibility listicles you are reading and where each publisher ranks itself. Run each prompt three times, in a fresh session, spread across at least two days. AI answers are non-deterministic, so the same jury can return a different verdict an hour later. Report your mention rate as a range across those runs rather than a single number. One pass gives you an anecdote, and three passes give you something you can defend in a meeting. Step 3: Score Mention Rate, Position, and Sentiment Capture three data points for every prompt: did your brand appear, where did it appear, and how was it described? Log all three for each platform. Mention rate is the percentage of prompts in your audit set where your brand appears. A 20% mention rate means you show up in 1 of every 5 queries. Track your top competitors on the same three axes. Note position carefully too, since first-position mentions get far more user attention than brands buried down the list. Pro Tip: Watch the Cross-Platform Sentiment Gap The same brand can show 0.769 sentiment on Perplexity and 0.052 on ChatGPT, a 14.8x gap, per Superlines’ 2026 data. Gaps like that usually trace to one specific source: a Reddit thread, a G2 review cluster, or outdated press. Audit which sources each platform cites and you’ll find the fix. Write your denominator down before you calculate share of voice. Ours is mentions divided by prompts times runs times platforms, so a 20-prompt library run three times across five platforms gives a denominator of 300. Every AI visibility tool reports share of voice and almost none of them publishes what it divides by. A percentage with no denominator can’t be compared against anyone else’s percentage. Step 4: Audit Technical Accessibility Check whether AI crawlers can read your site at all. Ugh, I know, robots.txt files. Do it anyway. The common blockers are overly restrictive robots.txt rules, CDN bot filtering, JavaScript-only rendering, and aggressive WAF settings. Any one of these can hide your best pages from the jury. Our guide to structuring a page so AI systems can quote it covers the on-page half of that work. While you’re in there, add or verify an llms.txt file at yourdomain.com/llms.txt. It’s a plain text file that gives AI systems a curated map of your most important pages. Treat it as a clarity signal; nobody has proven it moves rankings. Step 5: Audit Owned Content Structure Structure decides whether your pages get quoted. The often-quoted claim that well-organised headings earn 2.8x more citations traces back to AirOps citing itself, and the report it points at never mentions headings. The freshness figure is real and misattributed: SE Ranking measured 28% more citations for pages updated within two months, across 2.3 million pages. Check every high-priority page for five things: Direct-answer opening sentences FAQ schema dateModified timestamps Embedded citations and statistics A clear H2 and H3 hierarchy Step 6: Audit Your Off-Site Citation Footprint The jury reads Reddit. Per Semrush’s analysis , Reddit runs neck and neck with Wikipedia as the most-cited domain by LLMs. Audit your presence across Reddit, Quora, industry news outlets, editorial listicles, and review sites like G2 and Trustpilot. Document what you find, thread by thread. No published study supports the widely repeated claim that Reddit and Quora engagement lifts citations 4 to 7 times. I walked the trail on the pages that get credited for it. That’s the payoff for showing up where the jury does its reading. Step 7: Benchmark Against Competitors Score your top three competitors against the same prompt library and the same audit criteria. Every visible difference is a tactical opportunity. Look for the specific gaps: the Reddit threads they’re in and you’re missing, the third-party listicles that skip you. Those gaps become your work queue for the next quarter. Key Insight: Multi-Source Presence Beats Single-Site Authority The “2026 AI Search Visibility Report” credited across the web for a 2.8x multi-source citation lift was never published, and no publisher owns up to it. Multi-source presence still matters, and the honest version is that nobody has measured the size of the effect. That’s compared with brands mentioned only on their own website. Can AI Crawlers Reach You? Blocking GPTBot Does Not Remove You From ChatGPT Search This is the most common technical error in AI visibility advice, and pages ranking for this term state the opposite as fact. OpenAI runs one crawler for training and a different one for search. OpenAI’s crawler documentation puts it plainly. A webmaster can allow OAI-SearchBot “in order to appear in search results while disallowing GPTBot to indicate that crawled content should not be used for training OpenAI’s generative AI foundation models.” Google draws the same line for Gemini. Its crawler reference states that Google-Extended has no effect on a site’s inclusion in Google Search. So on three of the four major platforms, the training decision and the visibility decision are separate levers. Audit them separately, and check your CDN and firewall rules next to robots.txt, because a WAF can block a crawler your robots.txt welcomes. What Common Audit Findings Mean Scored worse than you hoped? Good, that means the audit is doing its job. Three patterns show up in almost every first audit, and each one has a known fix. Pattern 1: “We rank on Google but don’t appear in AI responses” This is the most common finding, and it traces to your citation footprint. The overlap between top Google links and AI-cited sources runs low, though the widely quoted “70% to below 20%” chain collapses under a check. Brandlight’s own site publishes 90% and 54% rather than those numbers, checked September 10, 2026. The 70/20 pair traces through LLMrefs’ 2026 GEO guide. The fix is off-site citation building: editorial listicles, Reddit threads, Quora answers, and earned media. My brand mentions vs citations guide shows how those sources feed the engines. The jury reads sources, and your Google rankings never enter the room. Pattern 2: “We appear in ChatGPT but not Perplexity (or vice versa)” Platform-specific gaps trace to which sources each engine trusts. Perplexity favors recent, well-structured content from authoritative sources. Microsoft Copilot leans on LinkedIn for B2B queries, and Claude prefers long-form comprehensive guides. Work backward from the missing platform’s preferred sources. My guide on how LLMs choose which brands to recommend maps each platform’s habits. Pattern 3: “We’re mentioned but the sentiment is wrong” Good news: this is the easiest finding to fix, because it points at specific sources. One bad witness usually explains it: a critical Reddit thread, an outdated review cluster, or a negative press piece. Audit which sources each platform cites, then fix the source. Sentiment typically shifts within 4 to 8 weeks once the underlying source changes. Example: A SaaS Brand’s First Audit Findings A typical first audit finds an 8% mention rate on recommendation prompts and strong schema coverage. It also finds zero Reddit presence, plus three competitors sitting in four-plus listicles the brand isn’t in. The fix sequence: listicle inclusion first for the fastest impact, Reddit presence second, on-site content third. AEO vs GEO: Where Your Audit Findings Point Every finding in this audit sorts into one of two buckets. AEO, answer engine optimization, means structuring content so AI engines can extract direct answers. GEO, generative engine optimization, means building the authority signals LLMs use when they pick which brands to name. AEO fixes are on-site: schema, content structure, direct-answer formatting, llms.txt, and FAQ pages. They’re necessary, and they’re the easy part. I cover the full definition in my guide on what AEO is . GEO fixes are off-site: Reddit, Quora, listicles, news coverage, review platforms, and brand search volume. They’re the heavier lift and the higher impact. For the deeper strategic breakdown, read my comparison of AEO vs SEO and which one B2B brands should prioritize in 2026 . And the top 50 brands receive about 28.9% of all mentions in AI Overviews, per Ahrefs research . Brand mention volume is the closest thing this field has to a master variable. See whether the trail ends at a study or at the publisher’s own homepage. Frequently Asked Questions What is an AI search visibility audit? An AI search visibility audit measures how often your brand appears in AI responses, where it ranks, and how AI describes it. It identifies the gaps between how your brand should appear in AI recommendations and how it does today. The output is a baseline score and a prioritized fix list, which is exactly what our AI SEO services build for clients. How often should I audit my AI search visibility? Run a full audit quarterly and monitor your top 20 to 30 prompts weekly. Brand visibility can decline 35.9% in just five weeks without active monitoring, per Superlines research. Quarterly audits catch directional shifts, while weekly monitoring catches platform volatility; see my guide on how to track your brand’s ChatGPT citations . What’s a good AI visibility score? No sourced universal benchmark for a good AI visibility score exists. Semrush’s help documentation describes its own AI Visibility Score only as “a benchmark from 0-100”, read on October 6, 2026. Our own working target is a 20% mention rate on category-defining prompts, and we treat anything below 10% as a serious gap. Do I need a paid tool to audit my AI visibility? No, a spreadsheet, a 20 to 30 prompt library, and access to the major AI chats will do it. Paid tools like Profound, OtterlyAI, and Semrush One scale the process and add behavioral analytics. For most B2B teams manual is the right start; see my roundup of the best AEO tools for B2B marketers . Can ChatGPT run an AI visibility audit on itself? ChatGPT can give you one data point, and it can’t audit itself reliably. OpenAI’s ChatGPT search help page says ChatGPT “typically rewrites your query” and may use saved memories when it does. That page also says citations “can be incomplete, outdated, or incorrect”, so test in a temporary chat and repeat every prompt. Why does the same prompt give a different answer every time? AI models are non-deterministic, so identical prompts return different wording, different brands and different citations from one run to the next. Model updates, session history and regional routing move the answer as well. How many times should you run each prompt? Run each prompt at least three times, in fresh sessions, spread across two or more days. Report the range across those runs, because a single pass measures one roll of the dice rather than your visibility. Should you allow AI crawlers in robots.txt? Allow the search crawlers, then decide separately about the training crawlers. OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot and PerplexityBot are what put you in cited answers, while GPTBot, ClaudeBot and Google-Extended govern training and grounding. text: AI Search General SEO AI Visibility Audit: How to Measure Your Brand’s Presence in AI Search By Despina Gavoyannis Senior SEO Specialist at Ahrefs Reviewed by Ryan Law October 30, 2025 13 min read 77 Linking websites Article performance data from Ahrefs Contents 1. Compare your visibility to competitors to close gaps 8. Turn these insights into a strategy for AI visibility Add Ahrefs as a preferred source on Google Add Ahrefs as a preferred source Add Ahrefs as a preferred source on Google Add Ahrefs as a preferred source An AI visibility audit provides a structured approach for search and brand teams to assess how their brand shows up on platforms like Google’s AI Overviews, ChatGPT, and Perplexity. It measures where the brand is mentioned in AI search platforms, how often, how accurately, and based on which sources. Here’s a step-by-step process for how you audit your brand’s AI visibility today. Want to turn your AI visibility audit into a report for stakeholders? Download the AI Visibility Audit Report Template , a free resource to share visibility gaps, AI mentions, and opportunities for growth with stakeholders. It includes: An executive summary format for leadership reporting Scoring tables for AI + search visibility Competitor insights stakeholders may be interested in An action plan and notes section to document next steps Follow the process below to help you fill out each section with valuable insights. 1. Define the scope of your AI visibility audit Before benchmarking your AI visibility , start by defining exactly what you’re auditing and where. This scope determines how consistent and comparable your data will be across platforms and time periods. Here’s what to clarify: AI platforms : Which platforms will you include in the audit? (e.g., Google AI Overviews, Gemini, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Copilot) Entities : List all the brand entities and sub-entities to analyze , such as your company, products, authors, thought leaders, or executives. Regions and languages : Define geographic or linguistic scopes, especially if your brand operates internationally. Listing this information upfront avoids inconsistent baselines when comparing visibility across different AI models or reporting cycles. For example, there’s a difference between only tracking mentions of your main brand and tracking all connected sub-brands or entities as well. For Ahrefs, it could include: Entity Type Example Main brand Ahrefs Product brands Site Explorer, Brand Radar, AI Content Helper Proprietary features Patches, Keyword Intents, AI Keyword Translator Proprietary metrics Domain Rating, Traffic Potential Personal brands Tim Soulo, Patrick Stox, Ryan Law, Glen Allsopp Sub-brands Yep, Detailed SEO Once your scope is defined, you’ll have a clear foundation for benchmarking and a repeatable structure you can use for future audits. 2. Benchmark your current brand visibility in AI search The next step is to assess your current brand visibility in search. You can manually check your brand’s search visibility for free by: Asking similar questions as your customers on ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google. Comparing whether your brand appears in the AI responses, what’s cited, and how results differ. Checking monthly or quarterly to track visibility changes. However, manual checks can’t scale and are easily skewed by model updates or personalized responses. For consistent, comparable data, you can use a tool like Ahrefs’ Brand Radar to track visibility across multiple AI platforms in one go. Enter your brand and select the region you’d like to receive data for: Take note of how metrics like your brand’s mentions, citations, impressions, and Share of Voice change across various AI search platforms: Mentions : The number of times your brand is mentioned in AI responses. Citations : The number of times your brand’s website is cited as a source in AI responses. Impressions : An estimation of exposure based on how often responses containing your brand are shown in search results. AI Share of Voice : How often your brand is mentioned in AI responses compared to competitors. You can also benchmark whether people are searching for your brand in the Search demand tab: This graph shows how branded search interest changes over time. A rise in search volume means more people are actively seeking your brand, while growth in search query count indicates users are asking a wider range of questions about you (from brand-level queries to specific product or feature searches). Check out these metrics periodically to see how your brand’s visibility changes over time and to report the results of your optimization efforts. 3. Analyze branded AI responses for accuracy and sentiment Once you’ve gathered your benchmarks, it’s time to go deeper. Start by looking at all of the AI responses that mention your brand in the platforms you care about. Navigate to the AI responses report, selecting the AI index you care most about to begin your analysis: The responses will look like this in the dashboard, with bolded mentions of your brand: Try using these filters to help make the analysis easier: Use Case Filter Settings See what AI says about you for branded searches Query contains {your brand} See how AI talks about your brand in general Response contains {your brand} Analyze when AI uses your content as a source Citation contains {your domain} You can mix and match filters to deepen your analysis. Here’s a helpful guide with more filter combinations and tips worth trying out. As you go through the responses, you’ll start to notice patterns about how AI mentions your brand. For example, you might notice that your brand appears in a lot of comparative searches, but your content isn’t cited. This means that the AI platform sources information about your brand from competitors or third-party, neutral sites that have compared you to competitors. Other patterns worth paying attention to include: Accuracy : Is your brand information in the response accurate? Sentiment and framing : Is your brand presented in a positive, neutral, or negative light? Differentiation : Are any unique attributes and positioning of your brand present in the response, or is it generic information? Authority : Is your brand presented as the lead mention with the most authority compared to others? Call-to-action: Does the response make you the recommended source to guide the user on the next step in their journey? If you notice incorrect, outdated, or potentially harmful information about your brand, make a list of the queries, responses, and cited sources so you can overcome misinformation and brand inconsistencies . Repeat this process for every AI search platform you want to analyze. You may notice that different patterns emerge for each platform. 4. Analyze AI visibility for unbranded queries and topic associations There are two types of analysis you can do here. The first is to search for your brand and filter out queries that do not contain your brand name. In the filter settings, set it to “Query doesn’t contain {your brand}”: Then, analyze the Topics report to see what your brand is commonly associated with. You can see the exact responses about the topic that also mention your brand: For example, Ahrefs is closely associated with SEO topics such as keyword research, backlinks, and website traffic. In most cases, if you’re visible in AI responses, the core topics you want to be aligned with will be reflected here. But you can also follow through with the next step to help you identify topics you might be missing. Instead of doing a brand search, this time, only include the main topics you want to be found for: It can help to analyze one topic at a time if there are a few you want to check out. Then use the filters to remove any results that mention your brand in the query, response, and citations. Check out the Topics report again to find sub-themes you may want to connect to your brand. Look for gaps you’d like to close, like where your brand is: Not mentioned, but a competitor is Not strongly associated with important sub-topics in AI responses Missing content formats AI frequently cites (like guides, videos, reviews) Then, you can close the gaps on your website by either publishing new pages or improving the topic coverage of existing ones. You can use AI Content Helper for this. It analyzes your content and helps you identify essential topics to cover on each page. 5. Find your top-cited pages in AI responses Analyzing your brand’s top-cited pages reveals which content AI systems consider most authoritative, helping you understand, replicate, and expand the signals driving your visibility in AI search. There are two ways to find your most popular pages that are cited in AI responses. The first is to use a tool like Brand Radar, which shows you the exact queries and responses you’re cited for. The second is to analyze your page-level traffic from AI by using a tool like Ahrefs’ Web Analytics or GA4. Check your top-cited pages in Ahrefs’ Brand Radar Start typing your brand in Brand Radar and select the option to add variations: This will allow you to add your website as part of your brand entity: You can only see data about citations if you add a domain to track, so always double-check this setting if you can’t see any citation data in the dashboard. Then, navigate to the Citations tab in the dashboard and check out how many citations your brand has earned across different platforms: Clicking these values will take you to the responses that include citations. However, you can also check out the Cited Pages report if you just want to see the list of top-cited pages. In some cases, you’ll see a list of pages from your site and others that are cited in the same responses where your brand is mentioned. Use the filter to show only your domain: You’ll end up with a list of top-cited pages in descending order based on how many responses used the page as a source: Cross-check the top pages earning AI traffic in your analytics data The second method you can try is to check out your web analytics platform and analyze which pages are getting the most traffic from AI. Although you won’t be able to see the exact queries and responses driving these clicks to your website, you can still get an idea of which pages actually earn clicks. Just because a page is well-cited among AI responses does not mean people will click on it. You’ll need to have AI tracking in your analytics tool already set up to get this data. If you use Ahrefs’ Web Analytics, this is set up for you automatically: Look for a list of the top pages visited most from AI platforms: Cross-check these pages against those in Brand Radar. For each one, check the responses the page is cited in: This helps you spot which queries and responses drive the most clicks from AI search results to your site. Repeat the process across different AI platforms (e.g., AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity) to compare click-through patterns. 6. Identify your best brand mentions that enhance AI visibility A major aspect of earning brand visibility in AI is how others talk about your brand online. You can run a full audit to analyze your brand mentions everywhere people talk about you. Doing this will give you a holistic idea of the language patterns and knowledge about your brand that AI is likely to include in responses about you. If you’re working agency-side or just don’t have time to do the full process, try out this shortcut that will help you prioritize which online mentions to analyze first. Run an empty search in Brand Radar and use the filters to only include the AI responses that mention your brand: Then, check out the Cited pages report. You will get a list of all pages that AI cites for responses that mention your brand. For instance, Zapier and Reddit are frequently cited in responses that mention Ahrefs: You can check out the responses themselves for an idea of how your brand was mentioned. Then check out the content cited on these websites to see exactly if (and how) they mention your brand. This analysis is useful for: Spotting your best web mentions and how they influence the way AI also talks about you Identifying misinformation in AI responses and tracking down the exact source Seeing what content formats are frequently cited in your industry (and publishing similar posts) Partnering with websites that frequently get cited and often mention you favorably Learning how people (and AI) position you against your competitors This provides a prioritized list of web mentions that significantly impact how AI describes your brand. Replicate the best ones for quick-win visibility gains while also reaching out to those that may need updating. Once you’ve identified these influential mentions, the next step is to find gaps you can close or opportunities your competitors have yet to tap into. 7. Compare your visibility to competitors to close gaps To benchmark your brand’s AI visibility against competitors, search your brand and then add one or more competitors like so: You can also try out the AI suggestions to auto-populate your top competitors in AI search. In the Overview tab, you’ll be able to compare your AI visibility directly to each competitor you entered. You can see each brand’s visibility metrics like mentions, impressions, citations, and AI Share of Voice for each AI search platform. Hover over the platforms you care most about until you see this window pop up: Each option will take you to a pre-filtered view of the AI responses report. Only brand : This report will show you queries and AI answers where the only brand mentioned is the one you’ve selected. It is great for assessing brand-specific queries and responses. With others : This report shows queries and/or responses that contain all the brands you’re comparing. It is great for assessing topics that are likely to mention you alongside competitors. Others only : This report shows queries that only mention the other brands you’re comparing against. It is great for finding topics that mention your competitors but not you. Check out these reports periodically for insights into which competitors might be growing their AI visibility quickly. If you add a topic as part of the main search, you can also hone in on any specific topics where competitors are mentioned but your brand isn’t. Pay attention to the AI Share of Voice metrics to see who has the highest visibility share in responses about that topic. It’s also worth checking out the Cited domains and Cited pages reports to identify the top sources mentioning each brand. Look for websites that mention competitors more than you and see how you can increase your mentions within them, too. There are numerous possibilities here, depending on which competitive insights matter most to your stakeholders. 8. Turn these insights into a strategy for AI visibility By this point, you’ll have a clear picture of how your brand appears in AI search: what’s working, where you’re absent, and how you compare to competitors. The final step is turning those insights into action. Use your findings to prioritize next steps based on impact and effort: Fix: Correct misinformation or outdated brand descriptions Build: Expand content coverage for missing topics and formats that AI cites most Influence: Strengthen relationships with authoritative sites that AI relies on for citations Depending on the task, you may need to collaborate with other teams to help you implement these actions. For example, if you have a PR team, they may be able to reach out to publications and correct misinformation about the brand in other people’s content. If you need to seek approval before you can start implementing these actions, take the time to create a report for your stakeholders. Download our free AI Visibility Audit Report Template if you don’t already have one. Replace all the pink sections and summarize your key findings in scorecards and quick snapshots of key points. Finally, turn your audit into an ongoing cycle, ideally monthly if you have the bandwidth. Otherwise, quarterly will do. With AI search platforms changing as quickly as they are, and competitors scrambling to win the largest share of voice, it’s worth checking your visibility frequently. Record the same metrics as you did in step two so you can see how your visibility shifts over time. Final thoughts An AI visibility audit tracks how your brand is presented in AI search over time. It measures the volume of responses that mention your brand name or cite your website as a source. However, it also assesses qualitative signals like how your brand is represented. text: Most brands know their Google rankings. Far fewer know whether ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google's AI Overviews recommend them at all — and that gap is easy to miss, because nothing tells you it exists until a customer mentions it. An AI visibility audit closes that gap. It answers questions like: When someone asks ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google AI about our category, does our brand show up? What topics is our brand getting recommended on, and where are we missing? Is our current website health and content strategy set up to help us succeed in AI search? This guide shows you how to run that audit using Semrush's AI Visibility Toolkit. You'll measure where your brand appears across AI platforms, which content gets cited, and where topical gaps exist. Any marketer with Semrush access can run an AI visibility audit alone — it doesn't require an agency or a dedicated data team — and the process scales down for smaller businesses too. Don't have Semrush yet? Try our free AI visibility checker to get started without a commitment, or read our lighter-weight walkthrough if you want a faster starting point. What is an AI visibility audit? An AI visibility audit is a structured review of whether your brand is recommended in AI-generated answers — ChatGPT responses, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity summaries — for the prompts and searches most relevant to your category. AI visibility audits ask a different question than the ranking checks you already run: not just whether you rank, but whether AI systems trust your brand enough to name it. That depends on different inputs — crawlable and extractable content, consistent entity signals, and a track record other sources corroborate — which is what the rest of this audit measures. How to run an AI visibility audit Run an AI visibility audit by seeing how you currently show up in AI answers and where you’re missing from the conversation. Do that in six steps: Establish your baseline for AI visibility Identify your citation-worthy content Find topics and prompts where your brand is missing Analyze brand sentiment and the AI narrative Identify influential off-site sources shaping AI answers Check site-level issues that affect AI access Let’s explore each step. Step 1: Establish your baseline for AI visibility Establishing a baseline for AI visibility shows you if AI systems reference your brand name or cite your content as a source more than competitors. Start by opening AI Visibility Overview in the AI Visibility Toolkit to see how your brand appears in AI answers . This dashboard shows mention counts, cited pages, and distribution across AI platforms (ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, AI Mode, Gemini). Write down your brand's AI Visibility score, mentions, and cited pages. Use these high-level metrics to benchmark your site against your competitors. For Allbirds, we see 4.9K mentions and 1.9K cited pages. Compare this baseline against competitors using the Competitor Research tool to see how that baseline stacks up against your closest competitors. For a deeper walkthrough, see our guide to benchmarking brand mentions in AI answers . Step 2: Identify your citation-worthy content Your citation-worthy content — the pages already earning AI citations — tells you what to publish and optimize next. Navigate to the "Cited Pages" section in Visibility Overview. This shows which URLs from the domain are referenced in AI responses and how many prompts from the Semrush database each page currently gets cited for. In the Allbirds example, educational and comparison pages earn more citations than product or category pages. That's a signal to optimize the educational pages already earning citations and create more like them. Next, expand a page to see the prompts and whether the brand name is "Mentioned" or "Missed" within those answers that cite the page. Cited and mentioned : A visibility win Cited but not mentioned : An opportunity to update the page and get mentioned for this prompt, as long as other brands are getting mentioned Compare AI cited pages to SEO Top Pages Comparing AI-cited pages to your SEO Top Pages shows you which pages rank well in search but earn no AI citations — a clear list of high-traffic pages worth optimizing for citations too. You can use the Top Pages report to compare this to the pages that attract the most SEO traffic. Notice in the case of Allbirds, the organic traffic is mostly driven by collection and category pages. These pages already rank well in organic search, but that's not the same as being AI-citable: Collection and category pages are built for browsing, not for the concise, self-contained answers AI systems extract and cite. Now, optimize them for AI retrieval — add clear structure, use question-and-answer formats, and concise summaries that AI systems can extract and cite. Step 3: Find topics and prompts where your brand is missing Finding topics and prompts where your brand is missing (called AI visibility gaps ) reveals where AI recommends your competitors instead of you. In Visibility Overview, scroll to "Topics & Sources" and select " Topic Opportunities ." Each topic shows where AI-generated answers exist and attract demand. For Allbirds, high-volume topics like "Running Shoes" and "Diabetic and Neuropathy Shoes" show their competitors mentioned, but not Allbirds. Each topic can be expanded to reveal the specific prompts generating those answers. Take note of the missed prompts to identify questions that your existing content doesn't answer. Then, create content that addresses those questions clearly and directly.To find more related topics and prompts, along with their AI volume and relevance, use Prompt Research . Step 4: Analyze brand sentiment and the AI narrative Analyzing brand sentiment and the AI narrative helps you see which brands are framed positively, neutrally, or negatively. Unlike search results, AI doesn't rank brands by their URL. It can, however, describe a brand as an option with pros and cons alongside other options. Use the Brand Performance reports to review sentiment and share of voice compared to your rivals. In this snapshot, Allbirds is usually framed favorably (88%) and holds the largest share of voice (14%) in AI answers compared to the competition. You can navigate to the “Key Sentiment Drivers” table in the Perception Report to review the brand strength factors and areas for improvement. Step 5: Identify influential off-site sources shaping AI answers Identifying influential off-site sources shaping AI answers lets you find which sources have influence in your niche, so you can pinpoint where your brand needs to appear. AI-generated answers often cite third-party user generated content (UGC) platforms like Reddit, YouTube, Quora, LinkedIn, and Medium. Back in the Visibility Overview , check " Cited Sources " to see which external domains are most frequently cited across your core topics. The domains that appear most often are shaping how AI systems explain your category and which brands get named, so they're where your brand needs to show up. You can use this data to determine if it's worthwhile to invest in growing your brand on YouTube or managing your reputation on Reddit. Step 6: Check site-level issues that affect AI access Check for site-level issues that affect AI access so you can fix any errors that could be hurting your visibility. Run a quick scan with Site Audit 's free check, then go deeper with the full site-wide audit covering issues like the ones listed below. The "AI Search Health" feature checks structured data and AI crawler access directly. Common issues affecting AI visibility: Weak internal context : Links without descriptive anchor text reduce how clearly pages are framed for AI systems. Internal links also signal to AI systems which pages belong to which topics, so pages without that context are less likely to be associated with your core subject matter. Structurally isolated pages : Pages with only one incoming internal link are less likely to be referenced consistently Missing AI guidance file : A missing llms.txt doesn't block access, but removes a clear signal about how AI should interpret site content These issues don't stop AI systems from crawling your pages. They make most of those pages harder to use as sources, so AI cites only the handful that are clear enough. Fixing them makes more pages easier for AI systems to use as sources. How to deliver your AI visibility audit Deliver your AI visibility audit as a prioritized list of gaps, baseline benchmarks against competitors, and a clear next step for each. The most useful audits reveal patterns: where AI consistently includes or excludes a brand, which content types AI relies on, and how similar prompts are handled across the category. Here are three options for delivery: Document illustrated with screenshots : Combine key Semrush screenshots with brief comments of what each report shows and what it implies. Quick to generate and easy to share by email. Standardized PDFs with Semrush My Reports : Use Semrush’s My Reports templates to consolidate metrics in one branded format. Connect Google Analytics to include widgets for analyzing AI referral traffic . These are ideal for recurring client reports. Video walkthrough : Pair a written audit with a Loom recording or live presentation to explain how findings connect, highlight priorities, and clarify tradeoffs. Best when alignment is needed before action. Choose the format based on how much context your recipient needs to decide what to do next. What to do after your AI visibility audit After your AI visibility audit, you'll want to fix technical issues, improve citation readiness, and expand topic coverage. The roadmap for each of these will be unique for each business and situation, but here's a suggested starting point. Immediate (week 1) : Fix technical issues that limit AI access. Resolve problems affecting whether AI systems can access, interpret, or attribute your content. These fixes have site-wide impact and set the foundation for everything that follows. Near term (weeks 2-4) : Improve citation readiness. Focus on improving content that's not already cited. Make existing pages clearer, more complete, and easier for AI systems to reuse. Set up Prompt Tracking on your highest-priority prompts to monitor progress continuously, rather than waiting to manually re-run the full audit. Mid term (months 2-3) : Expand topic coverage. Address the topical gaps by building new content in those areas where your brand is missing. Turn AI visibility audit findings into clear priorities As AI systems increasingly shape how options are compared and recommended, many brands still lack visibility into why their brand appears in some answers and not others. With Semrush, AI search patterns become observable signals you can review, prioritize, and revisit over time. Run your AI visibility audit with Semrush before your competitors do, and stay ahead in your market.

title: The AI Search Audit: A 10-Step Checklist for Your Site — ContextOwl
headings: What are the ten checks, and in what order?
How to score it, and what to fix first
text: Key takeaways Ten checks cover the full surface that decides whether AI engines can find, read and cite your site: crawler access, rendering, entities, content, schema, prompts, accuracy, competitors, third-party presence and a Google AI Overviews baseline. Most of it is free and fits in an afternoon: a robots.txt read, a "view source" check, a handful of prompts typed into ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity, and two or three Google searches. Score every item pass or fail, not on a scale. A crawler block that's "only on the blog" is still a fail — it blocks the pages most likely to get cited. Fix crawler access and rendering first. Nothing else on the list matters if the bot reading your site can't reach or parse the page. Re-run the whole audit after any robots.txt edit, CMS migration or template change, and at least once a quarter otherwise — crawler lists and AI answers both drift. This is a general, do-it-yourself list, distinct from ContextOwl's own report, which runs a separate, deeper 11-check technical audit as part of a paid deliverable. What are the ten checks, and in what order? Run these ten checks in order, because each one assumes the one before it passed. There is no point checking whether your content answers a question if the crawler that would read it is blocked at the gate, and no point auditing brand accuracy before confirming the engines can reach your pages at all. The list below moves from access, to content, to competitive position, to a baseline you can compare against next quarter. 1. Crawler access What to check: Open yoursite.com/robots.txt and look for Disallow rules against the crawlers that feed AI answers: OpenAI's GPTBot and OAI-SearchBot , Anthropic's ClaudeBot and Claude-SearchBot , plus whichever of Google's crawlers you use for Search. ( ChatGPT-User and Anthropic's Claude-User are triggered by a live user request rather than automated crawling, so a robots.txt block on them may not even apply — check them anyway.) Pass/fail: Pass if none of the above is disallowed on the pages you want cited. Fail if any one is blocked anywhere on the site you care about — including a rule that was meant to be temporary. This is the single most common self-inflicted gap; see should you block AI crawlers like GPTBot for the tradeoffs before you change anything. Example row (filled in): Audit of a fictional site, run 9 October 2026. Checked lumenanalytics.example/robots.txt . Found: User-agent: GPTBot Disallow: /blog/ Result: FAIL. OpenAI's training crawler is blocked from the blog, which is exactly where buying-intent content lives. Fix: remove the Disallow line for GPTBot and OAI-SearchBot unless deliberately opting the blog out of model training, in which case block only GPTBot and leave OAI-SearchBot (the ChatGPT search/citation crawler) untouched. 2. Rendering What to check: Fetch the raw HTML of a key page — curl it, or use your browser's "view source," not the rendered DOM in dev tools — and see whether your main heading and body copy appear in that raw response, or only after JavaScript runs. Pass/fail: Pass if the primary content is present in the initial server response. Fail if the raw HTML is a near-empty shell and the content only appears client-side. 3. Entities What to check: Is your brand name, product name and one-line category description consistent across your homepage, your About page, and the handful of third-party sources an engine is likely to pull from (Wikipedia or Wikidata if you have an entry, LinkedIn, Crunchbase, G2)? Check for Organization schema too. Pass/fail: Pass if the name and description match across at least three or four sources. Fail if your homepage, your LinkedIn and your directory listings each describe you differently, with no single consistent version anywhere. 4. Answer-ready content What to check: For each of your three to five core pages, can you point to one sentence near the top that directly answers the question a buyer would type — "What is X," "How much does X cost," "Who is X for"? Pass/fail: Pass if a standalone sentence answers the question within the first two paragraphs. Fail if the answer is implied, scattered across the page, or buried under scene-setting copy. 5. Schema What to check: Run your most important pages through a structured-data validator (such as Google's Rich Results Test) for Organization , Product , FAQPage or Article markup. Pass/fail: Pass if valid schema is present with no errors on the pages that matter most. Fail if there's no schema, or schema that throws errors. Note that Google's own guidance says structured data isn't required for its generative AI features specifically — this check is about general findability and rich-result eligibility, not a generative-AI requirement. 6. Buying-intent prompts and cited sources What to check: Ask five to ten buying-intent prompts in your category — without your brand name — on ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity, in fresh, logged-out sessions. Log which sources get cited for each. Pass/fail: Pass if at least one of your own pages is cited as a source in at least one engine for at least one prompt. Fail if only competitors' pages ever show up. See how to measure AI visibility for how to structure this logging so one lucky run doesn't look like a trend. 7. Brand accuracy What to check: Ask each engine directly: "What is [brand]?" and "What does [brand] cost / do / serve?" Compare the answers to your actual facts. Pass/fail: Pass if there's no material factual error — wrong price, a dead feature, the wrong audience. Fail if at least one answer states something false or outdated about you. Full method here: how to check what ChatGPT says about my brand . 8. Competitor gaps What to check: Using the same prompts from step 6, note every source cited for a competitor that never appears for you — comparison pages, review sites, documentation, forum threads. Pass/fail: Pass if you share most of the same cited sources as your competitors. Fail if competitors are consistently backed by a type of source — reviews, comparisons, docs — that your brand has none of anywhere. 9. Third-party presence What to check: Search your brand name plus "review," "alternative" and "vs," and see whether you appear on the directories, comparison sites and forums that typically surface as citations in your category — G2, Capterra, Reddit, trade directories. Pass/fail: Pass if you're present and reasonably current on at least two or three of the sources your category's engines tend to cite. Fail if you're absent from all of them, or present with stale or wrong information. 10. AI Overviews baseline What to check: Search three to five of your highest-intent Google queries, logged out and in an incognito window. Record, with a screenshot and the date, whether an AI Overview appears and whether you're named or linked in it. Google's own guidance points to the Search Console "generative AI performance report" as a way to monitor this over time. Pass/fail: Pass simply means a dated baseline now exists, whatever it shows. Fail means the step was skipped — the point of this one is having something to compare against next quarter, not a verdict today. For the mechanics of Google's generative features specifically, see the Google AI search optimization guide . How to score it, and what to fix first Count your passes out of ten. 8–10: A solid technical foundation. Spend your next afternoon on steps 6–9 — the competitive and prompt-level work — rather than re-checking access. 5–7: Real gaps worth prioritizing before any content or outreach push. Below 5: Stop and fix steps 1 and 2 before anything else. A perfect answer on a page a crawler can't reach is invisible regardless. Fix order, independent of score: crawler access and rendering (1–2) always come first, because every other check assumes a bot can reach and parse the page. Entities and schema (3, 5) come next — they're cheap, one-time fixes. Answer-ready content (4) follows. Steps 6–9 require ongoing prompt testing and real-world presence-building, so treat them as the recurring half of the audit rather than a one-time fix. Step 10 is a baseline you can log at any point, but keep it dated so it's comparable later. How to repeat this audit Re-run the full ten steps after any robots.txt change, CMS or template migration, or major rebrand — any of those can silently flip a pass to a fail. Otherwise, a quarterly cadence is reasonable: AI answers vary run to run even when nothing on your site changed, so a single pass or fail on steps 6–10 is a snapshot, not a permanent score. Keep each run's dated log rather than overwriting the last one, so you can see whether a gap is closing or just noisy. FAQ How long does this audit actually take? Most of it fits into a single afternoon: robots.txt and view-source checks take minutes each, the schema validator run is quick, and the prompt-based steps (6–8) are the only part that takes real time, since each needs several prompts across more than one engine. Do I need any paid tools to run it? No. A robots.txt file, your browser's view-source, a free structured-data validator, and chat interfaces for the major engines cover all ten steps. Which check should I fix first if I only have time for one? Crawler access. If a bot is blocked, nothing else on this list matters, because the content behind that block is invisible regardless of how good it is. Is this the same as ContextOwl's own technical audit? No. This is a general, free checklist anyone can run by hand in an afternoon. ContextOwl's full report runs a separate, deeper 11-check technical audit alongside prompt-based testing, delivered as a paid one-time report — the two lists aren't interchangeable. What if an engine gives a different answer the next time I run the same prompt? That's expected, not a bug in the audit. Treat steps 6–8 as a snapshot and log the date; a single run passing or failing is a data point, not a verdict, which is why repeating the audit matters more than any one pass. What to do next Block an afternoon and run all ten checks against your own site, logging each as pass or fail with today's date. Fix crawler access and rendering first — every other item on the list depends on a bot being able to reach and parse the page. Re-run the full audit next quarter, or immediately after any robots.txt, CMS or template change, and compare against today's log. This checklist is general guidance, not a report on your specific site; for a quick read on whether AI crawlers can reach yours, try the AI Bot Access Checker . Selling into India specifically? title: AI Search Audit Checklist: 40 Checks (Free Template)
headings: What is an AI search audit?
How long does an AI search audit take?
Is an AI search audit different from an SEO audit?
How often should I run an AI search audit?
text: Short answer: an AI search audit checks whether AI systems can access your site, understand who you are, find clear answers to your customers' questions, trust you based on third-party signals, and mention or cite you in practice. Work through the 40 checks below in six areas: access, content, structure, entity and consistency, reputation, and measurement. Fix access and accuracy issues first, then content, then reputation. Copy these checks into a spreadsheet with columns for status (pass, partial, fail), notes, priority and owner, and you have a working audit template. Many checks overlap with good SEO , which is intentional: AI search builds on the same foundations, with extra emphasis on clarity, consistency and third-party reputation. 1. Access (checks 1–8) robots.txt allows the search and user-triggered AI crawlers you want (for example OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, PerplexityBot, Claude crawlers) according to your policy. See AI crawlers explained . Googlebot and Bingbot are not blocked from important pages. CDN, firewall and bot-protection rules are not blocking legitimate AI crawlers. Important pages are indexed in Google (Search Console) and Bing (Bing Webmaster Tools). XML sitemaps are submitted to Google and Bing. Key content is in HTML text, not only in images, PDFs or client-side scripts. Pages load quickly and work on mobile. Important pages do not use nosnippet or restrictive snippet settings unintentionally. 2. Content (checks 9–18) A list of the top 20–50 customer questions exists and each has a clear answer on the site. Service and product pages state what you offer, who it is for, where, and price ranges where possible. Key sections start with a direct answer in one or two sentences. See answer-first writing . Headings reflect real questions. Passages are self-contained and name their subject. Comparison and "best for" content exists for common decision questions. Content includes specific facts, figures and examples, with sources where relevant. Authors and reviewers are named with credentials, especially for health, legal and financial topics. Pages show last-updated dates and time-sensitive facts are current. There is original content that others could cite, such as data, research, tools or case studies . 3. Structure (checks 19–24) Organization or LocalBusiness structured data with name, logo, address, contact and social profiles. Article, Product, Service or FAQ structured data where appropriate. Structured data matches visible content and validates without errors. Clear internal linking connects related topics (topic clusters). Breadcrumbs and logical URL structure. Multilingual sites (Urdu, Arabic) use separate URLs and correct hreflang . 4. Entity and consistency (checks 25–31) Business name, description and services are consistent across website, social profiles and directories. Google Business Profile is complete and accurate for each location. Bing Places is claimed and accurate. Apple Business Connect is claimed where relevant. About page clearly explains who you are, history, team and credentials. Founders and key experts have consistent public profiles (for example LinkedIn). Wikipedia or Wikidata entries (if they exist and are legitimate) are accurate; do not create self-promotional entries. 5. Reputation and third-party presence (checks 32–36) Reviews on Google and the main review platforms in your industry are recent and numerous. Your brand appears in reputable lists, comparisons and directories for your category. You have coverage or mentions in respected publications or industry sites. You know which third-party sources AI assistants cite for your category, and you are present on them. Outdated or inaccurate third-party information about you has been corrected where possible. 6. Measurement (checks 37–40) A prompt set is tracked monthly across ChatGPT , Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI features. See how to track AI visibility . GA4 has an "AI assistants" channel. See AI traffic in GA4 . "How did you hear about us ?" includes an AI assistant option. Results are reviewed monthly with actions assigned. Running the baseline test Before fixing anything, record how AI assistants currently describe you. Ask each platform three questions: "What is [your business]?", "Is [your business] good for [service]?" and "Who are the best [service] providers in [city]?". Save the answers with dates. This baseline shows whether descriptions are accurate, which competitors appear and which sources are cited, and gives you something to compare against after improvements. How to prioritise findings Priority Examples Critical Crawlers or Bing blocked; site not indexed; AI describing you inaccurately in damaging ways High Missing answers to top customer questions; inconsistent business information; weak reviews Medium Structured data gaps; no comparison content; no original data Ongoing Third-party mentions, PR , community participation, monthly tracking What an audit should produce A baseline of current AI visibility (mention rate and share of voice). A list of technical blockers. A content plan answering priority questions. A list of third-party sources to target. A measurement setup and reporting rhythm. Want a professional audit? Our AI search optimisation service starts with a full AI search audit and prioritised plan. For costs, see what AEO and GEO services cost . Frequently asked questions What is an AI search audit? A review of how well AI systems can access, understand, trust and recommend your business, covering technical access, content, structure, consistency, reputation and measurement. How long does an AI search audit take? A small business audit can take a few days; larger sites with many locations, languages or products can take several weeks. Is an AI search audit different from an SEO audit? They overlap heavily. An AI audit adds checks on AI crawler access, Bing visibility, entity consistency, third-party citations and AI visibility tracking. How often should I run an AI search audit? Once or twice a year, with monthly tracking of visibility in between. Can I do it myself? Yes, using this checklist and free tools. Specialists help with interpreting results, larger sites and building third-party presence. What tools do I need? Google Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools, a crawler, a structured data validator, access to ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini, and a spreadsheet. Paid AI visibility tools help at scale but are not essential to start.

text: The short answer An AI Search audit is a documented review of a defined prompt sample, the answers it produced, the sources shown with those answers, and the claims a team wants to make about them. It is not a single score and it is not a shortcut to a universal AI ranking. Use this sequence: scope → prompt → answer → source → claim → action → retest A good audit answers four questions: What exactly was tested? What did the answer actually say and cite? Which claims are supported, uncertain, or contradicted? What is the smallest defensible next action? Keep prompt context, answer evidence, source review, and the resulting decision in one auditable chain. This checklist targets practical searches such as “how to audit AI Search visibility,” “what should a GEO audit include?”, and “how do I verify AI citations?” It is an evidence framework, not a claim that any edit guarantees a mention, citation, recommendation, click, or revenue outcome. What an AI Search audit can and cannot establish Google’s documentation says AI features in Search use the same foundational SEO requirements as Search generally and that appearing in AI features is not guaranteed ( Google Search Central: AI features and your website , checked September 16, 2026). This supports an accessibility and content-quality baseline. It does not publish a universal citation formula. OpenAI documents web search as a tool that can return citations and sources ( OpenAI Developer Docs: Web search , checked September 16, 2026). That describes a documented OpenAI implementation; it does not make results from every AI surface interchangeable. The independent research paper GEO: Generative Engine Optimization evaluates visibility in generative-engine responses ( Aggarwal et al., arXiv , checked September 16, 2026). It is useful research context, not proof that a commercial metric predicts business results. Audit observation It can support It cannot prove by itself Brand appears in a captured answer Presence in that defined sample Universal market visibility Brand is recommended Recommendation language in that answer Product quality or buyer satisfaction URL is cited A source appeared with the answer A click, visit, or conversion Crawler requests a page An identified request in server logs That the page was used in an answer Answer changes after an edit A before/after pattern under recorded conditions That the edit caused the change The 30-point AI Search audit checklist A. Scope and decision: checks 1–5 1. Name the decision. Are you checking factual accuracy, category discovery, source coverage, competitor representation, or traffic attribution? 2. Define the unit of observation. Is one row one prompt run, one answer, one cited URL, or one claim-to-source relationship? 3. Set the market. Record country, language, city or region when relevant, and any personalization context that is available. 4. Separate surfaces. Keep ChatGPT Search, Google AI features, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, and other products separate unless an aggregate is explicitly labelled and reproducible. 5. Set the evidence rule. Define what counts as a mention, recommendation, citation, source position, absence, failed run, and non-comparable run before collecting results. Do not call a prompt panel “the market.” It is a sample designed for a decision. A small, stable panel can be more useful than a larger panel with mixed intent, markets, and definitions. B. Prompt design: checks 6–10 6. Assign a stable prompt ID. Use an ID such as CAT-014 rather than relying on a changing spreadsheet row. 7. Preserve exact wording. “Best enterprise GEO platform” and “GEO platform for a two-person agency” are different questions. 8. Label intent. Use consistent groups such as problem, category, comparison, branded, evaluation, local, or transactional. 9. Version meaningful changes. A new market, language, surface, or materially different wording should create a new version. 10. Keep branded and unbranded prompts separate. A product-fact query tests identity and accuracy; it does not test category discovery. A prompt is part of the measurement contract. If it changes silently, a later “trend” may simply be a different question. C. Answer capture: checks 11–15 11. Save the collection date and time zone. Answers and source sets can change. 12. Record the surface and mode. Record model or version only when the product discloses it; otherwise write not disclosed . 13. Preserve the answer. Save a permitted export, transcript, or capture reference before reducing it to a metric. 14. Separate mention, recommendation, and citation. A brand can be mentioned without an owned URL being cited. 15. Store exact source URLs. A domain-only label loses the page-level evidence needed for review. If a platform does not expose a field, write not available . Do not infer model routing, location, or source order from a dashboard label. D. Source and claim review: checks 16–21 16. Map each source to a claim. Record what sentence or product fact the URL appears to support. 17. Classify provenance. Use first-party, independent, community, commercial comparison, vendor-selected customer evidence, or unclear. 18. Check relevance. Does the source answer the prompt’s intent, or is it merely adjacent? 19. Check factual accuracy. Compare product facts, prices, integrations, and limitations with current primary documentation. 20. Check freshness. Record publication, update, or access dates when available; stale pages can still be indexable. 21. Check bias and incentives. A competitor, affiliate, agency, or vendor-selected case study may be useful but should not be presented as neutral evidence. A source can be relevant without being independent. A vendor case study can document what the vendor says happened, but it is vendor-selected customer evidence , not independent proof of a general result. E. Technical and measurement checks: checks 22–26 22. Check the canonical destination. Follow redirects and record whether the cited URL still resolves to the intended page. 23. Check access separately. Review robots directives, response status, rendered content, and server logs as adjacent evidence—not as an answer transcript. 24. Check the denominator. Report matched runs, failed runs, unavailable captures, and excluded prompts. 25. Check parser or product changes. Ask whether the monitoring tool changed its citation definition, source extraction, or historical calculations. 26. Reconcile with analytics carefully. A citation, crawler request, referral, and conversion are different events and require separate measurement. Google’s Search documentation is useful for foundational technical guidance, but an indexed page is not guaranteed to appear in an AI answer. Likewise, a crawler request does not prove that a page was cited. F. Interpretation and action: checks 27–30 27. Label confidence. High confidence requires complete context and answer/source capture; a summary score alone is low confidence for diagnosis. 28. State what remains unknown. Missing model, location, raw answer, or source relationship should lower confidence. 29. Choose one bounded action. Correct one stale fact, clarify one comparison criterion, fix one access issue, or schedule a matched retest. 30. Predefine the retest. Keep the prompt, market, surface, and collection rules stable enough to interpret the next sample. An audit is successful when a reviewer can inspect the evidence and understand the limitation. It does not need to end with a positive visibility result. A practical audit record Use one row per answer or claim-to-source relationship: observation_id: prompt_id: prompt_version: intent_group: exact_prompt: surface_and_mode: model_or_version: market_and_language: collected_at: answer_capture: mention_status: recommendation_status: cited_url: claim_supported: source_class: source_relationship_or_bias: accuracy_status: confidence: next_action: retest_date: A useful accuracy status is supported , outdated , unclear , or contradicted . A useful confidence scale is: High: complete answer and source capture, stable context, and claim checked against a current source. Medium: answer and context captured, but a key field or source relationship is incomplete. Low: summary metric only, incomplete answer, unknown context, or one unreplicated observation. Confidence describes the quality of the record. It does not describe the probability of a future citation or business outcome. How to audit a reported AI Search score When a vendor or agency gives you a visibility, share-of-voice, citation, or position report, ask for the measurement contract before interpreting the headline: Which prompts, versions, markets, languages, and surfaces were included? What is the exact denominator, and how are failures handled? Does “visibility” mean a mention, recommendation, source link, or another event? Are exact answer captures and URLs available? Are source position and domain-level visibility separated? Are branded prompts separated from category and comparison prompts? What happens when a parser or platform integration changes? Can the report distinguish a vendor-selected source from an independent one? Can the result be exported for a human accuracy review? Which claims are observations, and which are editorial interpretation? Tools can reduce collection work. AI Search Console , Peec AI , Otterly.AI , PromptWatch , and Profound describe different workflows and should not be assumed to calculate identical metrics. During a trial, compare raw answer access, exact source URLs, prompt versioning, surface context, failed-run handling, and export fields—not only the dashboard score. What to do when the audit finds a problem If the answer contains an incorrect product fact Verify the claim against the current first-party page, pricing or documentation page, and any relevant independent evidence. Correct the canonical source if it is inaccurate or ambiguous. Then record the change and retest the same prompt. Do not claim that the correction caused a later answer change unless the design supports that conclusion. If a competitor is recommended instead Capture the criteria used in the answer and the supporting sources. The right action may be a clearer comparison page, better documentation, or an independent source gap—not automatically more keywords. A recommendation is evidence about one answer, not a verdict on product quality. If the owned page is absent from citations Check whether the prompt is matched, whether the answer cited any sources, whether the page is accessible and current, and whether another URL from the same domain was used. One absent citation is a lead for investigation, not proof of a visibility loss. If the report claims traffic or revenue impact Request the separate analytics and attribution evidence. A citation can coexist with a referral, but the citation alone does not prove that the user clicked, converted, or generated revenue. FAQ How often should an AI Search audit be run? Use a cadence that matches the decision and the volatility of the facts being checked. A stable weekly or monthly panel is easier to compare than frequent runs with changing prompts. Pricing, availability, and other high-risk facts may justify additional reviews. Is an AI Search audit the same as an SEO audit? No. They overlap on technical accessibility and content quality, but an AI Search audit also preserves answer-level observations, source URLs, recommendation language, and the evidence boundary between citations and visits. Neither audit guarantees visibility. How many prompts should an audit include? There is no universal number. Start with the intent groups that matter to the decision, keep the denominator explicit, and add prompts only when they represent a defined question. More prompts do not repair mixed definitions or missing answer captures. Can I use a single AI visibility score? You can report an aggregate if its prompts, surfaces, weighting, missing-data rules, and definitions are documented. For diagnosis, keep surface-level observations separate because an aggregate can hide disagreement between systems. Does adding schema guarantee AI citations? No. Structured data can help communicate page information when it is accurate and eligible, but the sources checked here do not establish a universal rule that adding schema guarantees an AI citation or recommendation. Sources and verification The following sources were checked on September 16, 2026: Google Search Central: AI features and your website — official guidance on AI features and foundational Search practices; it does not publish a universal citation formula. OpenAI Developer Docs: Web search — official documentation for an OpenAI web-search tool and its citation/source fields; it does not establish equivalence with other surfaces. Microsoft Bing Webmaster Guidelines — official webmaster resource for Bing; it is a technical/search guidance source, not evidence of a universal AI-answer ranking. Aggarwal et al., “GEO: Generative Engine Optimization,” arXiv — independent academic research context; it does not validate a commercial score or guarantee a production outcome. Last reviewed: September 16, 2026. Data confidence: High for the linked official and academic source descriptions; medium for the checklist, which is AICiteKit editorial guidance and should be adapted to the fields each platform exposes.
