text: Nov 12, 2026 GEO 15 min read AI Search Audit: 13 Checks and Their Sources Read with AI Your site ranks fine on Google, yet ChatGPT and Perplexity never cite it when they answer questions in your niche. Before blaming the content, rule out the technical causes: AI crawlers may not get in at all, or they may get in and find an empty page. This checklist splits the work into 13 checks in 4 layers, notes how much official backing each one has, and runs 7 of them on linusseo.com with this site’s free tools. Most AI search checklists treat every item as equally important, so llms.txt and AI-specific structured data sit next to robots.txt. The backing behind them is very different. Some checks come straight from OpenAI or Google documentation, some are industry habits, and Google’s 2026 guide says a few of them are not needed at all. So each check below says where its backing comes from: the vendor’s official docs, third-party research or common industry practice. Key points An AI search audit has 4 layers: can crawlers get in, can they read the content, can they use it, and is anyone visiting or citing it. If the first two fail, nothing in the later layers matters. In 2026, check your CDN settings first, then robots.txt. Since September 15, 2026, Cloudflare’s Block options also block Googlebot. Crawlers come in three kinds: search, user-triggered and training. Blocking training crawlers does not stop AI search from citing you. OpenAI, Perplexity and Google say their user-triggered fetchers may ignore robots.txt. Google’s 2026 guide says you do not need llms.txt, content “chunking” or special structured data. Leave those for last. The fourth layer now has first-party data: Bing’s AI Performance report, GA4’s AI Assistant channel and Search Console’s generative AI report. What changed for AI search audits in 2026 A technical audit used to have one reader, Googlebot. Now each AI company runs its own crawlers, and four things changed. Crawlers split into three kinds with different rules. OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s crawlers each fall into three groups by purpose: a search crawler (such as OAI-SearchBot), a fetcher for pages a user asks the assistant to open (such as ChatGPT-User) and a training crawler (such as GPTBot). Perplexity runs only the first two and says PerplexityBot is not used to train models. Sites that block OAI-SearchBot are not shown in ChatGPT search answers, while blocking GPTBot only opts the content out of training. User-triggered fetchers are different again: OpenAI, Perplexity and Google say they may ignore robots.txt, and only Anthropic states that all of its bots follow it. The blocking point moved from robots.txt to the CDN. Since July 2025, new domains joining Cloudflare are asked during setup whether to allow AI crawlers, and the default option is to block them. Since September 15, 2026, Cloudflare’s Block options also stop Googlebot, Bingbot and Applebot, because those crawlers collect data for both search and training. A correct robots.txt can still be overridden by one CDN toggle that removes the site from Google Search and AI search together. Crawlers started proving who they are with signatures. Web Bot Auth lets a crawler prove its identity with a cryptographic signature instead of a User-Agent string, and the IETF chartered a working group for it in October 2025. ChatGPT’s agent browser already signs its requests. Since May 30, 2026, Shopify applies its strictest rate limits to unsigned bots. The fourth layer has first-party data. In 2026 Bing Webmaster Tools launched an AI Performance report, GA4 added a default AI Assistant channel, and Search Console added a generative AI performance report and an opt-out control. Before that, the only ways to check AI citations were asking the assistants yourself or paying for a third-party tool. For practitioners: 2024–2026 timeline 2024-12-17: Vercel and MERJ publish log research showing the major AI crawlers do not render JavaScript ( Vercel ). 2025-07-01: New domains joining Cloudflare are asked during setup whether to allow AI crawlers, with blocking as the default ( Cloudflare ). 2025-08-29: Shopify lets merchants authorize audit tools with Web Bot Auth ( Shopify changelog ). 2025-09-24: Cloudflare launches Content Signals with search, ai-input and ai-train ( Cloudflare ). Around 2025-12-09: OpenAI rewrites its crawler docs, and the robots.txt section no longer covers ChatGPT-User ( PPC Land ). 2026-02-10: Bing Webmaster Tools launches AI Performance in public preview ( Bing ). Around 2026-03-20: Google-Agent joins Google’s list of user-triggered fetchers ( Google ). 2026-05-13: GA4 adds an AI Assistant channel to the default channel group ( GA4 Help ). 2026-05-15: Google publishes its guide to optimizing for generative AI features ( Google ). 2026-05-30: Shopify tightens rate limits for unsigned bots ( Shopify ). 2026-06-03: Search Console launches the generative AI performance report and opt-out control, worldwide from August 31 ( Google ). 2026-09-15: Cloudflare’s Block options start covering Googlebot, Bingbot and Applebot ( Cloudflare ). Four layers, in order of how badly things break The layers come in order. If layer 1 fails, crawlers never get the page; if layer 2 fails, they get an empty shell. Fix those first; most of their checks are backed by official docs. Layer 3 mixes official requirements with checks that are only industry practice, so pick what is worth your time. Layer 4 is measurement, to confirm the earlier fixes worked. Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode use the regular index built by Googlebot. Google says there are no additional requirements to appear in them beyond being indexed and eligible for a snippet. Many checks below therefore matter most for ChatGPT, Perplexity and Claude, which do not use Google’s index. Layer 1: can AI crawlers get in? 1. robots.txt treats the three kinds of crawler separately Check that robots.txt does not block AI search crawlers by accident. A common mistake is trying to block training and adding OAI-SearchBot to the Disallow group as well, or blocking everything with User-agent: * . OpenAI, Anthropic and Perplexity each list their crawlers’ names and purposes in their official docs. The usual approach is to allow search and user-triggered crawlers and decide on training crawlers based on how you want your content used. Anthropic’s names are the easiest to mix up: Claude’s search crawler is Claude-SearchBot, and ClaudeBot is for training only. Two more names are control tokens: they never fetch pages and only declare data use in robots.txt. Blocking Google-Extended affects training and grounding for Gemini and other systems, not Google Search or AI Overviews. Blocking Applebot-Extended affects only Apple’s model training, not Siri or Spotlight. In this site’s AI Crawler robots.txt Checker , enter your domain and the path of a real article. It applies RFC 9309 to more than 30 crawlers and flags the ones whose operators say they may ignore robots.txt. Result for this site : all 31 crawlers are allowed and no common mistakes were found. 2. The CDN, firewall and platform do not block AI crawlers This is the most important check in 2026, and Google’s own documentation asks you to allow crawling in robots.txt “and by any CDN or hosting infrastructure”. Places to look: Cloudflare : open AI Crawl Control for the domain and check the Search, Agent and Training settings. Block or Block on pages with ads also blocks Googlebot, Bingbot and Applebot. If you only want to stop training, use Disallow AI Training. Other CDNs and firewalls : look for rules that block bot or AI categories, and for custom rules that match User-Agent strings. Shopify : bot protection rate-limits unsigned crawlers. To audit your own store with an SEO tool, generate a Web Bot Auth signature for the tool in the admin. This site’s What AI Crawlers See tool requests a URL once each with a normal browser, Googlebot and 5 AI crawler User-Agents. If the browser gets a 200 and an AI crawler gets a 403 or a challenge page, a rule is blocking by User-Agent. Result for this site : all 7 User-Agents got a 200 with the same bytes the browser received, so the hosting layer does not block these crawlers by User-Agent. 3. Verify real crawler visits against official IP ranges The simulation in check 2 only changes the User-Agent, and its requests do not come from the crawlers’ published IP ranges. Many firewalls check both, so passing the simulation does not prove real crawlers get in. To confirm, filter your server or CDN access logs by each vendor’s published IP list and look at the status codes those requests received. This site’s AI Crawler Log Analyzer takes an access log and separates real crawlers from impostors using the official IP lists. Anyone can fake a User-Agent, so counting by User-Agent alone can include impostors in your AI crawler numbers. For practitioners: published crawler IP lists OpenAI: https://openai.com/searchbot.json , gptbot.json , chatgpt-user.json , plus adsbot.json added in 2026 (OAI-AdsBot only visits landing pages of ChatGPT ads). Perplexity: https://www.perplexity.ai/perplexitybot.json , perplexity-user.json . Google: verify Googlebot by reverse DNS or the official IP lists; Google-Agent has its own user-triggered-agents.json . Anthropic discourages IP blocking; its verification list is at claude.com/crawling/bots.json . Apple: reverse DNS *.applebot.apple.com , IP list at search.developer.apple.com/applebot.json . Layer 2: once in, can they read the content? 4. Main content and internal links are in the raw HTML In 2024 Vercel and MERJ analyzed access logs and found that none of the major AI crawlers render JavaScript; only Googlebot (which Gemini also uses) and Applebot do. One or two sources claim that OAI-SearchBot has started rendering JavaScript, but OpenAI has not said so publicly. Agents that operate a page for a user, such as ChatGPT’s agent browser and Google-Agent, are real browsers and do run JavaScript, but the crawlers that build AI search indexes still do not. Content, prices, reviews and FAQs loaded by scripts are therefore likely invisible to the crawlers of ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity. This finding comes from third-party research; the AI companies have not described it themselves. The second section of the What AI Crawlers See tool parses only the raw HTML without running JavaScript. It counts visible text, headings, links and JSON-LD, and shows the opening text an AI crawler reads. Paste the text you copied from the rendered page and it estimates how much of it the raw HTML covers. Result for this site : the raw HTML of the English keyword research guide has about 5,000 words of visible text, 1 H1, 5 H2s, 16 H3s and 93 links. This site is static HTML generated by Hexo, so the text is in the HTML by design. Still, in the Semrush JS Impact report for the Site Audit guide , 191 of 193 pages changed after rendering, mostly in outlink counts and the word counts of tool pages, so even static sites are worth a spot check. 5. noindex, nosnippet and similar directives are not misused These directives decide how much of a page AI features can use: Google : according to Google’s documentation on AI features, noindex removes the page; nosnippet , max-snippet and data-nosnippet limit the text AI Overviews and AI Mode can show. Bing and Copilot : Bing’s 2026 webmaster guidelines say NOARCHIVE keeps content out of Copilot answers, and NOCACHE limits Copilot to the URL, title and snippet. However, on October 30, 2026 Bing announced two new preferences, ai-training and ai-grounding , and after March 1, 2027 it will no longer read NOARCHIVE and NOCACHE as preferences for training or grounding. Apple : Apple’s updated documentation says nosnippet also keeps content from being used as context for AI answers. Look for template-level settings, such as a theme that adds max-snippet:0 to every post. The third section of the What AI Crawlers See tool lists these directives for the page. Result for this site : the meta robots on posts is index, follow, max-image-preview:large, max-snippet:-1, max-video-preview:-1 , with no restriction. 6. Search Console’s generative AI control is set to include Search Console has a control that excludes a site from AI Overviews, AI Mode and AI features in Discover. It has been available worldwide since August 31, 2026. Google’s announcement says it is not used as a ranking signal for the rest of Search, but sites that opt out get no impressions or traffic from those AI features. When you take over a site, confirm the previous owner did not switch it off. It does not cover training, which is still controlled by Google-Extended. Layer 3: once read, can they use it? 7. Structured data matches the visible content Google’s guide says structured data is not required for generative AI search and there is no special schema.org markup to add. However, Google’s general structured data guidelines say not to mark up content that is not visible to readers, and Bing’s 2026 guidelines say markup must accurately reflect visible content; Bing adds that structured data may support clearer grounding but does not guarantee visibility. So this check is about consistency, and adding more markup does not help. Do price, stock, author and dates match between JSON-LD and the page, and does the same author or brand use the same @id across pages? This site’s Schema Visualizer draws JSON-LD as a relationship graph and checks common errors. To compare author and brand nodes across several pages at once, use the Entity Consistency Checker . 8. The page’s dates agree A page usually carries several dates: datePublished and dateModified in JSON-LD, meta tags, the date shown on the page, lastmod in the sitemap and the HTTP Last-Modified header. Google says it uses lastmod only if it is consistently accurate. The idea that AI search prefers fresh content is only industry speculation with no official statement, so the point of this check is to keep systems from misreading a page’s age, not to chase citations by changing dates. The fourth section of the What AI Crawlers See tool lists the dates from JSON-LD, meta tags, <time> elements, the visible text and the HTTP Last-Modified header side by side. It does not read the sitemap, so check lastmod by opening the sitemap separately. Result for this site : the structured data, meta tags and visible dates agree. The HTTP Last-Modified header is another matter. This site is hosted on Vercel, and both a 2023 post and a profile photo that has not changed in weeks report a Last-Modified from the day of the latest deployment, so the header says nothing about when content changed. 9. Each section opens with its answer The common advice is to answer in the first sentence under each heading, keep paragraphs short and cite sources for numbers, because AI answers often quote a single passage. This helps readers too, but the evidence is industry observation, and Google’s 2026 guide says you do not need to break content into small chunks or rewrite it for AI. Do it when you update old posts anyway. This site’s AI Citability Checker splits an article at its H2s and H3s, checks each section’s first sentence, length, numbers and sources, and explains what backs each suggestion. Result for this site : for the English keyword research guide, the opening sentence is a statement. The suggestions include a 355-word intro with no list or subheading and sections whose numbers have no source. The article does have a takeaways box, but the tool reported none because its list of labels does not include “Key points”, the label this site uses. 10. llms.txt (can wait until last) llms.txt is a Markdown index at the site root that lists a site’s important pages for AI. There is no evidence that the major AI search products use it. Google’s John Mueller said in 2025 that no AI system currently uses llms.txt, Google’s 2026 guide lists it among things you do not need, and the crawler docs of OpenAI, Anthropic and Perplexity do not mention it. It can make sense for developer and API documentation, which coding assistants may read; online stores and content sites can skip it. You can check the format with this site’s llms.txt Validator & Generator . Result for this site : this site has an llms.txt with 0 errors; the one tip is that its links do not point to Markdown versions. This site keeps it to test the tool and does not expect it to bring citations. Layer 4: is anyone visiting or citing it? 11. AI crawlers and user-triggered fetches in your logs Access logs answer two questions. First, did AI search crawlers visit, which pages did they fetch, and what status codes did they get? That verifies layer 1. Second, which pages did user-triggered fetchers such as ChatGPT-User, Claude-User and Perplexity-User open? According to OpenAI and others, these requests happen when a user asks something and the assistant needs to open a page. It follows that the pages they fetch most often are the pages AI actually uses in answers. That is this article’s inference; no vendor has published how these fetches relate to final citations. 12. AI Assistant traffic in GA4 According to GA4 Help, since May 13, 2026 GA4’s default channel group has an AI Assistant channel: when the referrer is a recognized AI assistant, the medium is set to ai-assistant . Google has not published the full list of assistants, and according to third-party tests the channel does not backfill and visits without a referrer still land in Direct. ChatGPT adds utm_source=chatgpt.com to its links, so ChatGPT traffic is easier to identify. In June 2026 GA4 also added a Source Group dimension, mainly to group sources such as social media by platform; it also has built-in groups for ChatGPT and Perplexity. To cover sources the default channel misses (such as Kimi or Doubao), pick them in this site’s AI Traffic Attribution: GA4 / Shopify Rule Generator . It generates the regex for a GA4 custom channel group and versions for Looker Studio, GTM and server logs. 13. Search Console and Bing AI reports Bing Webmaster Tools AI Performance : Bing’s official blog announced the public preview in February 2026. It shows how often the site is cited in Copilot and Bing’s AI summaries, which pages are cited and the grounding queries (the phrases the AI used to retrieve content). Third-party reports say a citation share metric was added in June. There is no click data. Search Console generative AI performance report : Google announced it on the Search Central blog in June 2026, and it has been worldwide since August 31. It shows impressions in AI features by page, country and device. It has no queries or clicks, combines AI Overviews and AI Mode, and the same data is also counted in the regular performance report. Both reports show which pages AI uses, but not clicks. For clicks, go back to GA4. On Cloudflare, open AI Crawl Control and make sure no Block option is stopping Googlebot. On Shopify, watch how bot protection treats third-party tools. Block training crawlers only and allow search crawlers. If you do not want your content used for training, block training crawlers and tokens like Google-Extended, and allow search and user-triggered crawlers. This does not stop AI search from citing you. Keep the content in the raw HTML. If a front-end framework or app loads your content, spot-check at least the product, category and article templates. Leave the checks that are only industry practice (checks 9 and 10) for last, and connect the layer 4 data first. A few weeks after fixing the first three layers, check the Bing and Search Console AI reports and GA4’s AI Assistant channel for changes. FAQ Does blocking Google-Extended remove my site from AI Overviews? No. Google-Extended controls Gemini training and grounding and does not affect Google Search, AI Overviews or AI Mode. To leave AI Overviews and AI Mode, use Search Console’s generative AI control, or nosnippet and noindex , which also affect regular results. Can robots.txt stop ChatGPT from opening my pages? Not completely. robots.txt controls OAI-SearchBot and GPTBot, but OpenAI says ChatGPT-User may not follow it, and the same goes for Perplexity-User and Google-Agent. Only Anthropic states that Claude-User follows robots.txt. To block those fetchers, you have to block their official IP ranges at the server or CDN. Everything passes. Why am I still not cited? This checklist only checks whether AI can get and use your content. Whether you get cited also depends on whether your content says something others do not, whether other sites mention your brand, and how each AI system picks its sources. text: AI tools recommend businesses they can reach, read, understand and trust. This checklist covers those four things in order, with 20 checks you can run yourself in about an hour. For each one you’ll find why it matters, how to test it, and how to fix it. Work from the top. A problem early in the list can make everything below it irrelevant: perfect FAQ answers don’t help if ChatGPT’s crawler gets a 403 at the door. Part Checks What it decides Reach 1 to 5 Whether AI crawlers can get to your pages at all Read 6 to 10 Whether they find text, links and every page you care about Understand 11 to 15 Whether they can tell who you are, what you do and where Quote 16 to 20 Whether your pages give them answers worth citing and trusting Part 1: can AI tools reach your site? 1. robots.txt allows the AI search crawlers The crawlers that put you in AI answers are OAI-SearchBot (ChatGPT search), Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, Googlebot (AI Overviews and Gemini) and Bingbot (Bing, Copilot, and a source for ChatGPT search). They’re separate from the training crawlers such as GPTBot and ClaudeBot. Test: open yourdomain.com/robots.txt . Look for Disallow: / under any of those names, or under User-agent: * when none of them has its own group. Each crawler follows only the most specific group that names it, so a blanket * block catches every AI crawler you didn’t list. Fix: give each search crawler its own Allow: / group. The full list, with example files, is in which AI crawlers to allow . In our study of the top 10,000 sites, 54.5% of the sites that blocked an AI training crawler also blocked an AI search crawler, so this one is worth checking even if you think you only blocked training. 2. Your server answers them with the real page robots.txt is only a request. Firewalls, CDNs and security plugins can turn an AI crawler away with a 403, a 429 or a challenge page before it reads anything, while every browser gets through. Test: fetch your homepage with a normal browser user agent and again with an AI crawler’s, and compare the status codes. The free AI crawler checker does both fetches in one step. Fix: look for a “block AI bots” or bot protection setting at your CDN, host or security plugin, and turn it off for search crawlers. These switches often cover search and training bots together. 3. robots.txt exists and answers quickly A missing robots.txt is fine. Google treats a 404 as “no crawl restrictions.” A broken one isn’t: Google says that when robots.txt returns a server error or times out, it “stops crawling the site” for 12 hours while it retries, then falls back to the last copy it cached. Test: load the file a few times and check it returns a 200 in under a second, as plain text, not an HTML page. Fix: serve it as a static file, not through your app. If your host returns an HTML error page at /robots.txt , that’s worth fixing too, because crawlers can’t read rules out of it. 4. No nosnippet on pages you want quoted A nosnippet robots meta tag tells Google not to show any text from the page, and Google says restrictive settings like it “limit how your content is featured” in AI experiences. A low max-snippet value and the data-nosnippet attribute do the same to part of a page. Some sites also use a noai tag; it isn’t a Google standard, but check what you’ve set and why. Test: view the page source and search for nosnippet , max-snippet and noai . Check the response headers for X-Robots-Tag too. The meta tag checker shows tags and headers together. Fix: remove them from pages you want cited. They often come from an SEO plugin setting or a theme nobody remembers changing. 5. Important pages aren’t noindex A page with noindex drops out of Google, and so out of AI Overviews and Gemini’s search answers. Staging settings that reach production are the usual cause, and the homepage is the most expensive place for it. Test: the same source and header check as above, for your homepage, pricing, services and contact pages. In Google Search Console, the URL Inspection tool tells you whether each page is actually indexed. Fix: remove the tag, then click Request indexing in Search Console. Part 2: can they read what’s there? 6. Your main content is in the HTML When you open a page, your browser runs its JavaScript and draws it. Most AI crawlers don’t. A December 2024 analysis of AI crawler traffic on Vercel’s network found that “none of the major AI crawlers currently render JavaScript,” including OpenAI’s, Anthropic’s and Perplexity’s. If your text is added by scripts after load, those crawlers see an empty page. Test: right-click the page and choose View page source (not Inspect). Search for a sentence from your main content. If it isn’t there, AI crawlers probably can’t see it. Fix: turn on server rendering or static generation for public pages. The details by platform are in JavaScript and AI crawlers . 7. Navigation links are real links Crawlers find your pages by following <a href> links in the HTML. A menu built from buttons with click handlers, or one that only exists after JavaScript runs, leaves every page behind it undiscovered. Test: in the page source, search for the address of one of your main pages. It should appear inside an href . Fix: use plain links in your header and footer for every page that matters. 8. A sitemap lists your pages, cleanly A sitemap tells crawlers what exists. It also tells them what you think matters, so a sitemap full of redirects, errors and blocked pages wastes their time. Test: open yourdomain.com/sitemap.xml (or the path your robots.txt names). Spot-check that the URLs return 200 and match your canonical addresses. Search Console’s Sitemaps report shows errors. Fix: list only live, indexable, canonical pages, and make sure the dates in it change when the page changes. 9. Each page has one clear canonical address The same page at http:// , https:// , www and without www , or with and without a trailing slash, splits signals across copies. Test: check the <link rel="canonical"> tag on a few pages, and type each variant of your domain to confirm it redirects to one version. Fix: pick one version, redirect the rest to it with a 301, and point every canonical at it. 10. Pages load fast on phones Slow pages cost you visitors first and crawls second. Google counts speed as part of page experience, and its AI search guidance asks for a good experience “across devices.” Test: run your homepage through the free page speed checker , which uses Google’s own test. Fix: compress images, cut unused scripts and third-party widgets, and use a CDN. Image weight is the most common culprit on small business sites. Part 3: can they tell who you are? 11. Your homepage says what you do, for whom, and where AI tools build their picture of your business from your own words. A homepage that opens with “Elevate your potential” gives them nothing to work with. Test: read the first sentence on your homepage. Would a stranger know your category, your customer and your area? Fix: write one plain sentence, such as “Fernway Roasters delivers fresh coffee to offices in Portland, Oregon, on weekly plans for teams of 5 to 200.” Put it in the first screen, and as text, not inside an image. 12. Organization or LocalBusiness markup names your business Structured data states the facts in a form machines read directly: your official name, logo, website, and the profiles that are yours. Test: run your homepage through the schema checker or Google’s Rich Results Test. Fix: add Organization markup (or LocalBusiness if customers visit you) with name , url , logo and sameAs links to your real social and directory profiles. Check every sameAs URL opens your own profile, not a namesake. 13. Local businesses include address, hours and area “Open now near me” style questions depend on address, hours and service area being stated clearly. An AI tool that can’t find your hours may skip you or guess them. Test: check that your LocalBusiness markup has address , openingHoursSpecification and areaServed , and that the same details are visible on the page. Fix: add them, and keep them in step with your Google Business Profile. 14. Your name, address and phone match everywhere AI tools cross-check what they find. When your site, your Google Business Profile, Yelp and directory listings disagree about your address or name, the AI has to choose, and it may choose the old one. Test: search your business name and compare the first page of listings with your site. Fix: pick one exact form of each detail and update every listing to match. 15. Your pages have markup that fits them Product pages can carry Product markup, service pages Service, articles Article, and question pages FAQPage. Google’s rule is that markup must match the page: “all the content in your markup is also visible on your web page.” Test: run your key page types through the schema checker and compare each field with what’s on screen. Fix: add the right type, and remove anything in the markup that the page doesn’t show, such as old prices or hidden FAQ answers. Part 4: can they quote you, and trust what they quote? 16. Key pages answer questions directly AI answers quote pages that answer the question in a sentence or two. Put the question in a heading in the words people search, and the answer right under it. Test: list the five questions customers ask you most. For each, find the page that answers it and check the answer is in the first two sentences under a matching heading. Fix: rewrite answer-first. “The team plan is $32 a month for up to 20 people” gets quoted. “Pricing depends on your needs” doesn’t. 17. Pricing is on the site “How much does it cost” is one of the most common questions people put to AI tools. If your price isn’t published, the AI may quote a competitor’s, an old one, or one it made up. Test: search your site for your main prices. Are they on a page a crawler can reach? Fix: publish prices, or at least starting prices and what they include. If prices vary, say what they depend on and give a range. 18. Content shows when it was updated Fresh facts beat stale ones, and AI tools can’t tell how current a page is unless it says. Test: check that articles and key pages show a visible “updated” date, and that dateModified in the markup matches it. Fix: add both, and only change the date when the content really changes. 19. Articles name their author A named author with relevant experience gives readers, search engines and AI tools a reason to trust a page over an anonymous one. Test: check your blog and guides for a byline and an author page. Fix: add a byline that links to a short author page with the person’s role and experience, or name the team clearly. 20. About, contact and policy pages exist These are small, cheap trust signals. They show there’s a real business behind the site, and they answer questions people ask AI tools, such as “does this company offer refunds?” Test: confirm you have reachable About, Contact, Privacy and, if you sell anything, refund or terms pages, all linked from the footer. Fix: write them in plain words, with real contact details. After the checklist: check what AI actually says Passing all 20 makes you easy to read and easy to cite. It doesn’t tell you whether ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity actually name you, or whether what they say is true. For that, ask them the questions your customers ask, the same way each week, and count how often you appear. We wrote up how to do that by hand in check what ChatGPT says about your business . fernwayroasters.com Sample 72 of 100 Crawling 88 On-page 64 Speed 79 Structured data 46 3 critical fixes +14 after the top 3 One scan covers the technical checks above and ranks what it finds by impact. Run all of it at once The free scan from AI Search Analyzer runs 157 checks, including every technical one above, on up to 50 pages in about 30 seconds. It ranks what it finds by what matters most and gives each problem a fix. The AI visibility checker covers the last step, showing what each AI tool says about your business and checking those answers against your site. text: All Blogs AI Search Audit: A 9-Point Checklist for AI Readiness AI Search Audit: A 9-Point Checklist for AI Readiness AI Search Audit: A 9-Point Checklist for AI Readiness Spencer Duke Published November 9, 2026 An AI search audit is a structured review of whether ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, and other artificial intelligence (AI) assistants can reach a website, read it, describe the company behind it correctly, and cite it in their answers. The method runs 9 checks in order (crawl access, AI crawler permissions, sitemap quality, structured data, entity signals, answer-first formatting, on-page evidence, third-party citations, and measurement), scores each one 0, 1, or 2, and fixes the lowest scores first. The audit applies anywhere an assistant composes the answer itself, including Google Search's AI Overviews and AI Mode, OpenAI's ChatGPT search, Anthropic's Claude, Perplexity, and Microsoft Copilot. They reach your pages through crawlers such as Googlebot, OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot, and PerplexityBot, and the picture they form of you can draw on your site, schema.org markup, LinkedIn, and review directories. A site can rank well on Google while a firewall rule or an outdated profile keeps it out of the answers that business-to-business (B2B) buyers read before shortlisting vendors. In this article you'll learn what an AI search audit is and how it differs from a classic SEO audit, the 9 checks that cover access, how to score each one, and what to fix first so the rest of your work actually shows up in AI-generated answers. Key Takeaways An artificial intelligence (AI) search audit checks 9 things in a fixed order, starting with crawler access, because a page an assistant can't fetch can't be cited however strong its content is. OpenAI documents separate crawlers for model training (GPTBot) and ChatGPT search (OAI-SearchBot) and treats each robots.txt setting as independent, so opting out of training can leave search access intact. Google sets 2 conditions for a page to be linked as a source in AI Overviews or AI Mode, being indexed and being eligible for a snippet, and says no special schema.org markup or AI text file is needed. Google ignores the priority and changefreq values in an Extensible Markup Language (XML) sitemap and trusts lastmod only when it is consistently accurate, so sitemap quality comes down to clean uniform resource locators (URLs) and honest dates. Structured data should be audited for accuracy rather than volume, because Google asks that every marked-up value match the visible text on the page. A baseline of fixed buyer prompts, recorded before any fix ships, is what lets you show afterward that the audit changed what assistants say about you. What Is an AI Search Audit? An AI search audit tests your site and wider web presence against the steps an assistant takes before naming a vendor: fetching pages, reading them, working out who you are, judging trust, and citing a source. Each test produces a score plus a saved piece of evidence, such as a screenshot or an exported report, so anyone can rerun it later. Know How It Differs From an SEO Audit A classic search engine optimization (SEO) audit asks whether Googlebot can crawl, index, and rank your pages. Some teams call the newer review a ChatGPT SEO audit or a large language model (LLM) SEO audit, but its scope reaches past your domain. Audit question Classic SEO audit AI readiness audit Which bots get tested Googlebot and Bingbot Googlebot and Bingbot, plus the search crawlers run by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Perplexity What gets reviewed Pages, templates, and rankings Pages, plus the individual passages an assistant could quote Where findings come from Your own domain Your domain, LinkedIn, directories, review sites, and publications Typical finding Broken links, slow templates, missing title tags A search crawler blocked at the firewall, or 3 different company descriptions online What it hands back A prioritized fix list A scored checklist, an evidence folder, and a prompt baseline What Should an AI Readiness Audit Check? It should check 9 areas that group into access, understanding, trust, and measurement. Work through them in order, because a failure near the top of the list hides every result below it. Use the 9-Point Checklist Treat this table as your answer engine optimization (AEO) audit checklist. Copy it into a spreadsheet, add a score column and a notes column, and fill in one row at a time. # Check Test to run Pass standard Evidence 1 Crawl access URL Inspection on 10 priority page addresses (URLs), plus bot status codes in content delivery network (CDN) or server logs All return 200, render main text, and pass the firewall Screenshots, log extract 2 AI crawler permissions Read robots.txt for OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, and the * wildcard No Disallow on pages you want cited Dated robots.txt copy 3 Sitemap quality Compare the Sitemaps report with your canonical page list Absolute canonical URLs, no redirects or 404s, honest lastmod Report export 4 Structured data Test 5 pages in the Rich Results Test or Schema Markup Validator Valid, and every value matches the page Validator results 5 Entity signals Compare company facts across About page, LinkedIn, and directories Matching name, category, products, and buyer Fact grid 6 Answer-first formatting Copy each section's opening into a blank document Each opening answers its heading alone Pass rate per page 7 On-page evidence Highlight every claim on 5 commercial pages Each claim has a number, date, source, or customer Marked-up copies 8 Third-party citations Log cited domains for 20 unbranded prompts on 4 assistants Present on 7 or more of the top 10 cited domains Citation log 9 Measurement Confirm a fixed prompt set, an AI referral channel, and log access All 3 exist with a dated baseline Baseline sheet Score Each Check 0, 1, or 2 Give 2 for a clean pass, 1 for a partial pass such as 7 of 10 pages, and 0 for a fail or a check nobody can run yet. Order matters more than the total of 18, so clear every 0 in rows 1 to 3 before touching content, since an assistant that can't fetch a page never sees it. How Do You Check Whether AI Crawlers Can Reach Your Site? You test 3 layers: whether pages render for bots, whether robots.txt admits the AI search crawlers, and whether your sitemap points them at the right URLs. AI crawler optimization starts here, because access often breaks through a setting changed for another reason, such as a security rule. Test Crawl Access Past Robots.txt A permissive robots.txt means little if your CDN challenges unfamiliar bots or key pages only show text after JavaScript runs. Google's AI features documentation asks owners to allow crawling in robots.txt and at the CDN or host, and to keep important content available as text. For each priority URL, open the rendered HyperText Markup Language (HTML) in URL Inspection and confirm the main copy is there. Then pull 7 days of server or CDN logs filtered by AI user agents, and use our server log method to tell verified crawlers from impostors. Audit AI Crawler Permissions One Bot at a Time OpenAI runs 3 agents: OAI-SearchBot surfaces sites in ChatGPT search, GPTBot collects content for model training, and ChatGPT-User fetches pages during certain user actions. OpenAI's crawler documentation treats each setting as independent and says search changes take roughly 24 hours, so blocking training alone leaves search access as it was. Anthropic and Perplexity name their own search crawlers, Claude-SearchBot and PerplexityBot. Open yourdomain.com/robots.txt , write down every User-agent group, and flag any Disallow that reaches a page you want cited, including rules under the * wildcard that apply to every bot. Grade Sitemap Quality Against Google's Rules Google's sitemap guidance caps each sitemap at 50,000 URLs or 50MB uncompressed, asks for fully qualified absolute URLs, and uses lastmod only when it is consistently and verifiably accurate. Google also ignores priority and changefreq, so tuning those values buys nothing. Compare the Sitemaps report export with your canonical page list and flag every redirect, 404, noindexed URL, and lastmod date that resets on each deploy. Confirm robots.txt carries a Sitemap line, and use our infrastructure checklist for canonical tags and internal linking. Does Structured Data Matter for AI Search? Structured data labels facts like your company name, authors, and publish dates for machines, but Google states that AI Overviews and AI Mode need no special schema.org markup. When you audit structured data for AI search, check accuracy rather than volume. Match Every Marked-Up Value to the Page Google's AI features guidance asks that structured data match the visible text on the page. Run 5 priority pages through Google's Rich Results Test or schema.org 's Schema Markup Validator, then compare each value, such as price, rating, author, date, and address, with what a visitor actually sees. Mismatches tend to appear after a price change or a rebrand, when the copy changed and the template didn't. Score the check 0 if any value contradicts the page. How Do You Audit Entity Signals? You list your core company facts, then check every place they appear, including assistants' answers about you. The goal is one consistent description that assistants can match to the right buyer questions. Build a Fact Grid Across Sources Make a grid with 6 rows (name, category, main products, target buyer, headquarters, and pricing model) and 1 column per source: your About page, LinkedIn, Crunchbase, your main review directory, and your press boilerplate. Mark every cell that disagrees with the About page. Score the check 2 if no cell disagrees, 1 for small wording drift, and 0 if any source names an old product, category, or buyer. Fix your own pages first, then send each profile owner the corrected wording. Ask Each Assistant to Describe You Ask ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Perplexity what your company does, who it sells to, and what it costs, with sources. Paste each answer into a new grid column to see where every assistant's version departs from yours and which page it cited. How Do You Audit Content for Answer-First Formatting and Evidence? Pick your 10 most commercial pages and run 2 tests on each: whether its passages stand alone and whether its claims carry proof. Both read the page the way an assistant quoting one passage would. Lift Each Opening Out of Context Paste the opening 2 sentences of each section into a blank document, leaving the heading behind. The passage fails if it leans on words like "this" or "as mentioned" for meaning, or never answers the heading. Divide passing openings by total openings and set a pass mark, such as 8 in 10. Rewriting openings costs less than new pages, so this fix often ships first. Score the Evidence Behind Each Claim On your 5 main commercial pages, highlight every claim about results, speed, savings, or customer outcomes. A claim passes when it carries a number, a date, a named source, or a named customer, and a visible author and publish date add context to the page as a whole. Score each page by the share of claims that pass, and list each unsupported one with the proof it needs. Adjective-heavy pages give an assistant nothing specific to repeat, so this list often runs longest. How Do You Audit Third-Party Citations? Run your category prompts on each assistant, record every domain the answers cite, and compare that list with where your brand appears. The gap between the 2 lists becomes your off-site fix list. Log Cited Domains by Assistant Write 20 unbranded prompts from sales calls and demo forms, such as requests for a vendor shortlist in your category. Run each in a fresh session on ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Perplexity, log every cited domain beside its assistant and prompt, and see our analysis of most-cited domains for how those lists shift by industry. Rank the Gaps by Overlap Sort the log by how many assistants cite each domain. Domains cited by 2 or more assistants that leave you out go to the top of the fix list, followed by domains listing you with outdated facts. Score the check 2 if you appear on 7 or more of the 10 most-cited domains, 1 for 3 to 6, and 0 for fewer than 3. A new listing counts only once an assistant starts citing it, so rerun the prompts after each outreach push. How Do You Measure Whether the Audit Worked? Record a baseline before you fix anything, then rerun the same prompts and checks on a schedule. Without that ninth check, the other 8 can't show progress. Lock a Baseline Prompt Set Save the 20 prompts from the citation check, add a few branded ones, and record for each assistant whether you were mentioned, cited, or recommended. Keep the list unchanged between runs and use our guide to buyer prompt research to choose them. Read the Reports You Already Have Search Console counts AI Overviews and AI Mode traffic in the Performance report under the Web search type, and its generative AI performance report shows impressions by page, country, device, and date. ChatGPT tags referral links with utm_source= chatgpt.com , so group AI referrals into one Google Analytics 4 (GA4) channel and compare it monthly. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) Can I Run an AI Readiness Audit Myself? Yes. Every check here runs on free tools: Google Search Console, a browser, the Rich Results Test or Schema Markup Validator, server logs, a spreadsheet, and the assistants themselves. The harder part is fixing what the audit finds, especially firewall rules, markup, and third-party profiles that need a developer or outreach. Should I Block GPTBot to Protect My Content? That depends on whether you want your content used for model training. OpenAI documents GPTBot as its training crawler and OAI-SearchBot as the crawler behind ChatGPT search, each set independently. Blocking GPTBot alone leaves ChatGPT search access unchanged, while blocking OAI-SearchBot keeps your pages out of those answers. Do I Need Schema Markup to Appear in AI Overviews? No special markup is required. Google's documentation sets 2 conditions for a page to be linked as a source in AI Overviews or AI Mode: being indexed and being eligible for a snippet. It adds that no special schema.org structured data is needed, though accurate markup still describes your company clearly. How Often Should I Repeat the Audit? Run the full 9-point audit once a quarter and after any migration, redesign, content management system (CMS) change, or new firewall setting, since those moments break access rules unnoticed. Rerun the prompt baseline monthly with identical prompts, so you can tell whether visibility moved because of your fixes. How Is an AI Readiness Audit Different From an SEO Audit? A search engine optimization (SEO) audit checks whether search engines can crawl, index, and rank your pages. An AI readiness audit adds the AI search crawlers, passage-level formatting, entity consistency across third-party profiles, and the domains assistants cite, then tracks mentions and citations across fixed prompts.
